label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 1 · drive · chip Far-sighted (was Shrewd)

options.text: Reading the real value of things is your standing talent, and it works on houses, people, and offers alike. You see the water damage behind the fresh paint and the good bones behind the ugly listing. Bad deals rarely survive your first slow walk around them.

You see a chance long before anyone else wants it. Having somewhere next to go is your safety, so you watch where a thing is heading more than what it is. Looking far costs you some of what is near, and the trade favors you.

You see what a thing will become before it looks like anything. Needing a way forward is how you feel safe, and that puts the far chance ahead of the near one. Trust that early sight, and keep track of what you already have.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_self · chip Far-sighted (was Shrewd)

options.text: Everyone else toured the staged interior. You spent nine minutes in the basement with a flashlight and offered twelve percent under asking, with reasons attached. The sellers argued, then folded. Two years later the neighbors are still asking how you got that price.

Looking far comes naturally, and it pays. The next place is clearer to you than this one, so you see the far chance sooner than the near one. You lose the opening at hand most, and one quick look before passing it keeps it.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_others · chip Far-sighted (was Shrewd)

options.text: You look past the people closest to you toward the next place. Seeing far is how you keep them safe, and that gives the plan more of you than them. If you let them look with you, you see far enough for all of them.

Friends bring you their contracts the way people bring jewelry to an appraiser. You flip straight to the page where deals go wrong, and you are rarely wrong about which page that is. Your fee is a coffee, and the savings have bought several people cars.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 2 · drive · chip Takes the chance (was Well-traveled)

options.text: Waiting for a better chance has never been your way. Being in motion steadies you, and it puts the chance you can take today ahead of any promised for later. Take it, and know that moving early means paying for a few that go nowhere.

Ground you have personally covered is your actual education. Markets, cities, kitchens, border towns: you learn places by standing in them, and every trip quietly becomes inventory. When a decision needs context, you usually have some, bought at the price of having been there.

A chance within reach is hard to leave alone, because standing in place feels like losing. You take the one that is here rather than wait for a safer one. You take them best with your eyes open, since some of them cost you.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_self · chip Takes the chance (was Well-traveled)

options.text: Taking the chance pays you more than waiting does. Moving makes you feel alive, so you put money into what moves rather than what is safe. Take the next one with money you can spare, because the wrong ones cost what the sure ones kept.

The supplier problem stumped the office for a week, and you solved it with one call to a man you met at a trade fair in 2021, in a city nobody else could place. The office called it luck. Your contact list calls it coverage.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_others · chip Takes the chance (was Well-traveled)

options.text: You take the chance for everyone whose money sits beside yours. Moving feels safer to you than staying, and you put their calm into the venture with your own. You take it for them too, and choosing its size with them costs you nothing.

People assume your stories are exaggerated until they travel with you once and watch three strangers in two cities greet you by name. The network was not built at desks. It was built at long tables, and it keeps paying for itself in favors.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 3 · drive · chip Shares the win (was Overflowing)

options.text: Plenty follows you around, and you spread it without doing the math. The garden overproduces, the table seats extras, the referral goes out before being asked for. Abundance is your operating assumption, and somehow the assumption keeps proving itself right.

A win only feels real to you once you have shared it. Providing is where you feel most yourself, and you share a good month rather than put it away. You share because it is right for you, and the thinner cushion is the price.

Sharing what you win comes more naturally to you than banking it. A win that stays with you feels unfinished, and that puts giving it away ahead of keeping it. Share it, and count what is missing from the bank as a price you chose.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_self · chip Shares the win (was Overflowing)

options.text: You came back from the weekend market with too much of everything, again, and by Sunday night four households had bags on their porches. Nobody keeps score, least of all you. Somehow your own porch is never empty either, which you have stopped calling coincidence.

Sharing the win is your natural generosity, and it leaves you short. What you give in a good year you lack in a lean one, because giving comes ahead of keeping. If you keep some of each win back, the lean year stops costing you.

label: 土_偏财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_others · chip Shares the win (was Overflowing)

options.text: You share each win rather than sit on it. Giving in bursts is your way of loving, and you hand them plenty one year and nothing the next. You do them more good sharing in a shape that lasts, since they come back.

Around you, people relax about money in a way they cannot explain. There is always somehow enough, and some extra, and a plan for the extra. Scarcity thinking finds no soil at your table, and guests leave having borrowed a little of your assumption.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 1 · drive · chip Chases every chance (was Land-hungry)

options.text: Every new chance pulls at you harder than the one you already took. You need the feeling of a beginning more than a middle, and chasing is how you get it. You chased the one you have now just as hard, and you know it.

Wanting more ground is a hunger that eating does not fix. The bigger house asked for a better car, which asked for the second property, which asks nightly for a third. Each acquisition was supposed to be the last one. The hunger signs nothing and remembers nothing.

The next chance always looks better to you than the one in your hands. Movement is how you feel alive, and you chase what is coming rather than work what is here. Keep in mind that you only keep what you stay to collect.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 1 · cost_self · chip Chases every chance (was Land-hungry)

options.text: You opened the property app at eleven again, two years after buying the place that was supposed to end the searching. Saved listings: forty-one. The current house, by any honest measure, is enough. Enough has somehow never once felt like the finish line it promised to be.

Chasing the next chance costs you the one you hold now. Each new start takes the strength the last one needs, and you would rather begin again than finish. You already know that the chance in your hands closes while you are off chasing.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 1 · cost_others · chip Chases every chance (was Land-hungry)

options.text: Friends hear about each new purchase with congratulations that have grown slightly careful. They can see the pattern you narrate as progress: the goalposts move the week you reach them. Somebody once asked what amount would finally be enough. The pause afterward answered better than you did.

You chase the next chance before anyone is out of the last one. You want starting more than staying, and you give the new venture what you owed the old one. Try to remember that you leave someone holding each chance you chase past.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 2 · drive · chip Spread too thin (was Never-settled)

options.text: You are spread across more things than any one of them can use. Saying no feels like losing, so you hold many small pieces rather than one whole thing. You give each one a part and none the whole, and that is worth remembering.

Spreading yourself across every venture feels safer to you than trusting one. One thing failing would take you with it, so you keep a piece of everything instead of the whole of anything. Notice that being this spread out keeps you busy rather than safe.

Staying put itches. Six months into any arrangement, your eyes drift to the exits: the next city, the next market, the next better setup. The moving was exciting the first several times. Somewhere along the way it stopped being motion toward anything and became the motion itself.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 2 · cost_self · chip Spread too thin (was Never-settled)

options.text: Spreading yourself thin keeps you from being caught out and keeps you tired. You give each venture enough to stay in rather than enough to win, since quitting feels like losing. Remember that you pay for all of them with the one body you have.

The boxes from the last move were still flat-packed in the closet when you started browsing rentals in a city you visited once. Your lease has eight months left. Your address book has three crossed-out entries per person, and your friends now write yours in pencil.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 2 · cost_others · chip Spread too thin (was Never-settled)

options.text: People love you from a slight distance, because the distance keeps changing. Invitations come with a built-in question mark, since nobody is sure which city you answer from this season. The freedom is real, and so is the pencil everyone writes your address in.

Wherever you can reach, you spread yourself across every person and plan. Keeping every option alive matters more to you than giving one your whole attention. Do not forget that you give each person in your plans the part of you the others left.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 3 · drive · chip Half-finished (was Spread-thin)

options.text: Starting a thing gives you more than finishing it. The beginning is where the feeling lives, and you spend your strength there rather than on the last stretch. You get nothing for the half until the rest is done, and you need no reminding.

You start at full strength and finish on what is left. Being new suits you better than being done, and the end asks for strength you spent at the start. Bear in mind how much of the value sits in the part you leave undone.

Your holdings outgrew your hands a while ago. The properties, the side hustles, the commitments across three time zones all technically function, and all of them get a thinner slice of you each season. Everything is covered. Nothing is tended. The difference is starting to show.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 3 · cost_self · chip Half-finished (was Spread-thin)

options.text: Finishing is what you save for later. The last stretch costs you more than the first, and you open a new thing sooner than you close an old one. Hold onto the thought that the money and the credit sit at the end you leave.

Sunday was for the rental’s leaky tap, the market stall’s inventory, the cousin’s business plan, and the neglected tax folder. Each got forty minutes and none got finished. You fell asleep mid-list. The tap is still dripping into a bucket that has its own schedule now.

label: 土_偏财 · friction · row 3 · cost_others · chip Half-finished (was Spread-thin)

options.text: You hand people a beginning and call it done. Starting is where you feel strongest, and you put everything into the first stretch instead of saving some for the last. Make a note that you give the people waiting your start and somebody else's finish.

From outside, your empire looks impressive, and up close it looks tired. Tenants wait longer, partners chase you for answers, and the best opportunity of last year slipped past while you were patching the worst one. Everyone can see the stretching except the person stretched.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 1 · drive · chip Makes things last (was Thrifty)

options.text: Getting full value out of things is a craft you practice daily and almost invisibly. The repaired instead of replaced, the bought-once-properly, the leftovers built into a second dinner. Waste offends you mildly and constantly, and your accounts show what mild constant offense saves.

Whatever you own, you keep working for years. Buying new feels like giving up on something, and that puts fixing ahead of replacing every time. Keep making things last, and let a few of them go while they still have worth to someone.

Making a thing last is a craft you practice without noticing. Waste feels to you like a small loss of control, so you repair what you own rather than replace it. You pay by living with the older version a while longer than you need.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_self · chip Makes things last (was Thrifty)

options.text: The winter coat is on its ninth season, re-zipped twice by the tailor whose name you know. Colleagues in this year’s jackets tease you about it. The retirement account you never mention could quietly buy everyone at the table a coat store.

Making things last keeps you in control of what you own. You put hours into repairs ahead of the better thing on offer, because replacing feels like waste. Once fixing costs more than the thing is worth, letting it go gives you those hours back.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_others · chip Makes things last (was Thrifty)

options.text: Nobody watched you be careful, and everyone sees what the care built. The coat is nine seasons old and the house is paid for, a math the flashy spenders around you have slowly started doing out loud. You never once explained it. The results explain it, late and completely.

You keep old things going for everyone around you. Fixing beats choosing for you, and you have the people at home living with your kept things rather than their own. You make the rest last, and one new thing a year is theirs to pick.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 2 · drive · chip Saves first (was Steady)

options.text: Saving comes first for you, ahead of the treat and the trip. A cushion is what lets you relax, and you put money away rather than enjoy it. Saving first suits you, and a few good things you were slow to buy are the price.

Holding course is your competitive advantage in a distractible world. The plan from January is still the plan in September, adjusted, funded, on schedule. Shiny alternatives pitch themselves at you weekly and bounce off politely. What you committed to, you finish.

Money feels like yours only after part of it is put away. Being covered matters more to you than being treated, and the saving comes before the spending. Keep that order, and spend one saved thing on yourself from time to time.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_self · chip Saves first (was Steady)

options.text: Saving first is the quiet skill under everything you own. You would rather be covered than pleased, and the good thing you can afford keeps waiting. If you spend one saved sum on something you want, the pleasure you put off stops being the price.

While the group chat cycled through four investment fads in a year, your boring monthly transfer went through forty-eight times, unphotographed. Two of the fads ended badly for people you love. Your account did the thing accounts are supposed to do, quietly, again.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_others · chip Saves first (was Steady)

options.text: You save for the people you love ahead of spending on them. A safe future is the gift you trust, and you give them the cushion rather than the dinner. Spend part of it on them this year, because it was for them all along.

People set their watches by your consistency and occasionally roll their eyes at it, until their own zigzags total up. Then they come asking about the boring transfer. You show them the math, kindly, without once saying the sentence you have earned.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 3 · drive · chip Loyal (was Well-stocked)

options.text: Being loyal costs you less than leaving ever would. The known thing keeps you safe, and you hold what is already yours instead of looking elsewhere. You stay a while past where it serves you, and that is the price of loyalty like yours.

Loyalty is your default, given before it is asked for. Choosing again asks less of you than starting fresh, and you place the person you have ahead of anyone new. Keep giving it, and let the few people you never met be the price.

Reserves are your love language and your strategy. The pantry, the savings, the spare parts drawer, the contact who owes you one: whatever the situation needs, some corner of your life already holds it. Emergencies visit you and find the door already answered.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_self · chip Loyal (was Well-stocked)

options.text: Your loyalty stays put, and it pays in people who stay. You keep choosing what is yours rather than ask if it chooses you too. Asking every so often costs you little, while loyalty to what does not love you back costs you closeness.

During the outage, your house was the one with candles, a charged power bank, cash, and cocoa. Three neighbors ended up in your kitchen playing cards by lamplight. It was, one of them said, the nicest blackout of their life. You had planned for worse.

label: 土_正财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_others · chip Loyal (was Well-stocked)

options.text: People tease you about the stockpiles until the day they call you from a breakdown lane, a storm, or a sudden expense. You always have the thing. Around you, disasters get downgraded to inconveniences, and nobody fully registers who did the downgrading.

Loyalty is how you love, shown by staying. You keep the one you have rather than look around, and you let the staying speak for you. Being chosen again is a thing you give out loud, and you give it less than you mean to.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 1 · drive · chip Keeps everything (was Hoarding)

options.text: What comes into your keeping stays there for good. Needing a thing you let go is the loss you fear most, and you store it for years rather than lack it once. You keep the fear along with the thing, and that bears repeating.

Keeping has stopped being a strategy and become a compulsion with a filing system. Money is stored rather than used, and might-need has annexed the garage. Security was the goal once. Now the piles themselves ask for protection, and you provide it nightly.

Letting a thing go is harder for you than keeping it. Having it within reach makes you feel safe, so you keep things for a someday need rather than a present use. Tell yourself plainly that everything you keep also has to be looked after.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 1 · cost_self · chip Keeps everything (was Hoarding)

options.text: Keeping everything is your insurance against going without, and it costs you. You would rather pay to store a thing than risk needing it, and your money guards what you never use. Let yourself see that you rent space for things that give nothing back.

The garage has not held a car since 2019. It holds four labeled bins of cables for devices you no longer own, kept because throwing them out feels like bleeding. You bought a fifth bin last month. The car sits outside in the weather, losing value.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 1 · cost_others · chip Keeps everything (was Hoarding)

options.text: Family negotiates with you before every clear-out, and loses. Guests notice the house has started belonging to its contents. The savings, which are genuinely impressive, work the same way: admired, counted, and never allowed out to actually do anything.

You hold onto things you cannot bring yourself to drop. You keep a thing rather than take its space back, and you fill the home from the walls in. Keep sight of how you charge the people at home for it in space.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 2 · drive · chip Hard to move (was Immobile)

options.text: Staying put feels like safety, whatever the place becomes. Moving asks more of you than staying, so you keep the known rather than go toward the better. Know that a place you will not leave is not one that holds you.

Your money and your life share one posture: seated. The cash waits in the account earning almost nothing, the career waits in the safe role, the plans wait for a certainty that never files its paperwork. Waiting feels responsible. Compounded, it has cost more than any risk would have.

You are hard to move, as you would say yourself. Leaving asks more of you than staying does, and you keep the job and home past their use. You choose to stay every day you do not leave, and that choice deserves a second look.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 2 · cost_self · chip Hard to move (was Immobile)

options.text: Being hard to move keeps your life steady and small. You would rather weigh a move than make one, and the better place is taken while you weigh it. Take it as given that the chance to go closes during the deciding.

The savings sat through two boom years at a fraction of a percent while you researched, thoroughly, the accounts you never opened. The research folder is excellent. The difference between it and action, calculated once by your brother-in-law, funded his kitchen renovation.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 2 · cost_others · chip Hard to move (was Immobile)

options.text: Advisors, friends, and one very patient cousin have all presented you the same numbers and watched them lose to inertia. Nobody doubts your discipline. They doubt the strategy of a fortress that never opens its gates, even to let its own supplies grow.

You stay, and hold the people closest to you in place. Staying matters to you more than moving somewhere better together, and you set the whole house to your speed. Ask yourself whether you make them wait on a move you are not making.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 3 · drive · chip Hates to spend (was Cheap)

options.text: You hate to spend, even on the things you can plainly afford. Spending feels like losing control, and you hold onto the money rather than buy what you wanted. Be honest with yourself about how much more you can afford than you let yourself have.

Spending comes hard to you, even on what you need. Money going out stings you most, and you go without rather than pay for the thing. You are allowed to pay full price for what you want, as you well know.

Spending hurts you in a place logic cannot reach, and the people around you absorb the difference. The heating waits until the frost, the tip gets calculated to the coin, the gift arrives practical and slightly under the occasion. The books balance. Warmth pays the levy.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 3 · cost_self · chip Hates to spend (was Cheap)

options.text: At the anniversary dinner you queried one item on the bill, correctly, for four dollars. The table went quiet in a way the four dollars did not buy back. Your partner said nothing then and remembered it at strange moments for a year.

Hating to spend means you rarely overpay and rarely enjoy. You would rather keep the money than spend it, since spending feels like a loss already begun. Keep it in view that you end up with the money and without the thing it was for.

label: 土_正财 · friction · row 3 · cost_others · chip Hates to spend (was Cheap)

options.text: Spending on the people you love comes no easier than spending on yourself. Giving less feels safer than giving more, and you make the saving on them. Spare a thought for what you save on them, since it comes out of their side.

People plan around your tightness with small workarounds: they book the restaurant, buy the better wine themselves, stop suggesting trips. You read it as everyone overspending. They read the flinch that crosses your face at every bill, and they have stopped bringing you their celebrations.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 1 · drive · chip Goes first (was Fast-climbing)

options.text: You go first, with the plan half done and the vote not in. Waiting your turn feels like losing, since the opening is worth more to you than certainty. You pay for going first in landings taken alone, and asking one person along changes that.

Going first is how you find out if a thing is real. Being bold costs less than being left behind, and you go ahead of knowing where you land. You spend yourself going first, and one turn handed away gives some of it back.

Upward is your body’s default direction, and speed is its signature. New job, new ladder, new wall: you find the holds faster than anyone expects, and you are halfway up before the group finishes stretching. Height that takes others years takes you seasons.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_self · chip Goes first (was Fast-climbing)

options.text: You joined in March as the junior hire and by December were running the standup, through momentum rather than coup. The org chart caught up to reality in the spring. Somebody checked the dates twice, assuming a typo. The dates were right.

Where the signal has not come, you have already gone. Being the one who moved counts for more than being the one who was ready. You take the first loss alone each time you go, and one person told beforehand would halve it.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 1 · cost_others · chip Goes first (was Fast-climbing)

options.text: Plan or no plan, you go first and let the rest catch up. Moving matters more than agreeing, and that puts your people a step behind their own decision. Wait one beat, because going first takes from them the chance to choose it with you.

Peers track your ascent with a mix of inspiration and vertigo. Some train harder because you exist, which you would take as the highest compliment. The ones who resent it are mostly resenting the mirror. You climb past both kinds without slowing.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 2 · drive · chip Loves a race (was Gutsy)

options.text: Nerve is your renewable resource. You ask for the number with a straight face, take the shot with the game on the line, sign up before feeling ready. Fear shows up on schedule and finds you already moving, which it never quite gets used to.

Whenever a race starts near you, you find new speed. Being compared reads as a reason, and you chase another's lead instead of starting from nothing. You love the race more than the finish, and letting one go costs you nothing you would miss.

A race wakes you up like nothing else. Having someone just ahead is your best fuel, since a pace you can see beats one you must invent. You race for the movement more than the win, and you can let one end without losing anything.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_self · chip Loves a race (was Gutsy)

options.text: Racing brings out your best and spends most of it. Being ahead feels better than being rested, and that comes out of a reserve that was never deep. You pay for each race in sleep not made up, and sitting one out costs you nothing.

You asked for forty percent above the posted range, out loud, in the actual meeting, while your co-applicants asked for the midpoint. The pause lasted four seconds. You got thirty-two percent and a reputation. Both are still compounding.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 2 · cost_others · chip Loves a race (was Gutsy)

options.text: People borrow your nerve for their own risky moments, asking what you would do and then, crucially, whether you would come along. You usually would. Half your circle’s boldest stories feature you standing just off-camera, having dared them into the frame.

You turn shared things into a race. Moving counts for more with you than winning, and that keeps the people beside you in motion long after their finish. You cost them the rest they came for by racing on, and letting one end returns it.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 3 · drive · chip Shares the risk (was Rivalry-fueled)

options.text: Given the choice, you put the stakes in a shared pot. Being in it together makes a risk worth taking, since a bet carried alone weighs more than one split. You share the risk ahead of sizing it, and one look is cheap.

Sharing the risk is the first thing you offer. You like a bet best with someone else's name beside yours, because carrying it alone turns daring into worry. You split the risk ahead of measuring it, and measuring first keeps the friendship whole.

Competition is your fertilizer. A rival in the field and your growth doubles: the training sharpens, the hours deepen, the work finds another gear you did not know the engine had. You do not resent your rivals. You privately thank them, at the finish line.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_self · chip Shares the risk (was Rivalry-fueled)

options.text: Whenever a venture needs a partner, you have already said yes. Going in together feels safer, and you would rather split a win than keep it whole. You share each loss as readily as each win, and the money not kept is your price.

The gym was dying at six in the morning until the newcomer started matching your pace. Within a month you were both twenty percent stronger and nodding like diplomats. Neither of you has ever named the arrangement. Both of you check the other’s numbers first.

label: 木_劫财 · catalyst · row 3 · cost_others · chip Shares the risk (was Rivalry-fueled)

options.text: Coaches and managers quietly use you as the pace car, placing you near whoever needs pushing. It works every time. The people you pull upward mostly like you, once they recover, and the record boards in several places carry the results of arguments you started.

Your bets carry other people's names. You would rather share the risk than own the call, and that puts their money where your nerve is. Whenever you count them in unasked, you take a choice they never made, and one question first gives it back.

label: 木_劫财 · friction · row 1 · drive · chip Bets too big (was Overreaching)

options.text: Your reach consistently files claims your foundations cannot fund. The bigger title, the second loan, the bet sized for the person you plan to become: each grab lands just past stable, and the wobble afterward is now a recognizable season of your life.

Betting too big is a reflex for you more than a decision. Winning small never feels like proof, and you raise the stake ahead of checking what sits under it. Keep in mind that only the bet you can afford to lose is really yours.

You size every bet past what the moment asks. More drive sits in you than one plan can use, and the extra goes into the stake instead of the base under it. Remember that a bet sized for next year is paid for this year.

label: 木_劫财 · friction · row 1 · cost_self · chip Bets too big (was Overreaching)

options.text: The renovation budget was set, then exceeded by the better tiles, then by the wall that became optional, then structural, then gone. The house is beautiful and the debt has a view. You have started describing year five of the two-year plan as phase two.

Where a smaller bet would hold, you put down the big one. Playing small feels worse than losing, and you take the big risk ahead of sure footing. You lose in money not kept the bet you did not need, a number worth remembering.

label: 木_劫财 · friction · row 1 · cost_others · chip Bets too big (was Overreaching)

options.text: Lenders, partners, and family have all developed the same small pause before your proposals. They have watched the pattern: brilliant start, stretched middle, scramble. They still say yes, usually at reduced exposure, and keep a quiet reserve for the scramble.

Your biggest bets land on other people too. Going big matters more than going safe, and that puts the shared money at your size of risk. Bear in mind that a bet too big for you is also a bet with their savings.

label: 木_劫财 · friction · row 2 · drive · chip Never stops racing (was Turf-guarding)

options.text: The finish is the one thing you cannot want. There is more of you than one race can use, and you keep running past the line instead of standing on it. Remember that no race ends on its own, and stopping is something you decide.

Your patch gets defended with energy the patch itself never asked for. The account, the role, the recipe, the driving route: colleagues, siblings, and once a wedding DJ have all met the fence unexpectedly. Sharing feels like shrinking. So the fence grows instead.

Whenever you finish, you look for the next race before the last cools. Staying put feels like being passed, and there is more go in you than a finish uses. You race the next instead of keeping the win, and the win was the point.

label: 木_劫财 · friction · row 2 · cost_self · chip Never stops racing (was Turf-guarding)

options.text: The new colleague suggested a small improvement to your process, and your reply, though polite, contained a full title deed. The improvement was good. It surfaced eight months later from someone else and you fought it again, on principle, before quietly adopting it.

Racing without a finish is the shape of your effort. You keep going past where rest would pay rather than let anyone pass you. You lose each win to the next race, and the rest you never take is the thing to remember.
